newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Congress panel to vote soon on Brazil telecom bill.
newsitem.headline: Congress panel to vote soon on Brazil telecom bill.

text.p: A final draft of a bill outlining the rules for the privatization of Brazil's telecommunications industry will be presented to a committee in the lower house of Congress on May 6 and could be voted on this week, a lawmaker said.

Deputy Alberto Goldman, who is in charge of the bill in the committee, said he believed it more likely, however, that the legislation would only be put to a vote by the panel in the week beginning May 12.
If approved in the panel, the legislation advances to the floor of the Chamber of Deputies where it is expected to be put to a vote quickly. It also requires Senate approval.
Goldman briefed reporters about changes to key articles of the bill and reaffirmed his intention not to place restrictions on foreign capital in the sector.

Instead, the bill would give the Brazilian president powers to limit the involvement of foreign capital on a case- by-case basis, depending on Brazil's trade relations with each country in question, the lawmaker said.
Such a move would give Brazil "bargaining power" in its attempts to remove trade barriers to its exports, Goldman said.
One important change included in the final draft would channel all funds raised from the sale of concession rights to the National Telecommunucations Agency, a new regulator.
The receipts, expected to total tens of billions of dollars, would be used to cover the agency's costs, ensuring it complete autonomy from the government.

Once those costs were covered, the remainder of the concession fees would be funneled into a so-called Universalization Fund, which seeks to widen public access to telecommunications and then to the National Treasury.
Goldman also said the agency would be given powers to undo what it considers to be concentration of ownership in the telecommunications sector.
Another article of the law would make the agency the only body responsible for overseeing the sector, ruling out the possibility of third-party contractors being hired to carry out specific tasks.
